Lightning talk

A Practical Guide to JVM Native Memory in Kubernetes

Carl Chesser
@che55er | che55er.io

The trap

Heap tuning is not container tuning

  • The heap is only one part of JVM memory.
  • Kubernetes limits appl to the whole OS process.
  • Native memory can quietly eat the headroom.

The symptom

More memory, same surprise

OOMKilled

The container crosses its memory limit, even when heap graphs look calm.

$$$

Teams raise requests and limits "just to be safe", then pay for unused capacity.

The real budget

What has to fit inside the pod limit?

0 Pod memory limit 100%
Heap
Threads
Meta
Direct
JVM
Margin
Java heap Thread stacks Metaspace/classes Direct buffers Code cache, GC, JIT Safety margin

Sizing goal

Use the container, do not pad it blindly

  • Oversized limits hide the problem and waste schedulable node memory.
  • Undersized margins turn native growth into OOMKills.
  • A good target is measured heap plus native memory plus explicit safety margin.
  • Right-size after load testing, then watch cgroup usage drift in production.

Useful framing

Think in container math


pod limit
  >= heap
   + native memory
   + safety margin

If you only set -Xmx, the rest of the process still needs room.

Kubernetes controls

Requests schedule, limits enforce


resources:
  requests:
    memory: "768Mi"  # scheduler reserves this much node capacity
    cpu: "500m"
  limits:
    memory: "1Gi"    # cgroup hard boundary for the process
    cpu: "1"

Requests ask Kubernetes to place the pod where at least that much capacity is available. Limits are the hard cgroup boundary the process must stay under.

Java 17+

The JVM now sees more of the container

  • Java 17 includes cgroups v2 support and container-aware OS metrics.
  • Heap ergonomics can size from the container limit, not the node.
  • JDK 23 and newer 17/21 updates expose better cgroup memory details in diagnostics.

First check

Prove the JVM sees your limit


java -XshowSettings:system -version
jcmd <pid> VM.info
java -Xlog:os+container=debug -version

Use the first two for normal checks; use logging when the JVM's view looks wrong.

Example

-XshowSettings:system surfaces cgroups


$ java -XshowSettings:system -version
Operating System Metrics:
    Provider: cgroupv2
    Effective CPU Count: 1
    CPU Quota: 100000us
    CPU Period: 100000us
    Memory Limit: 1.00G
    Memory & Swap Limit: 1.00G

This is the quick "am I sizing from the pod or the node?" check.

Read it

What those fields tell you

  • Provider: cgroupv2 means the JVM is reading Linux's unified cgroup hierarchy, available since Linux 4.5 in 2016.
  • Memory Limit: 1.00G is the ceiling for heap plus native memory.
  • Effective CPU Count: 1 influences GC threads, JIT threads, and application parallelism.
  • CPU Quota and CPU Period should line up with the deployment CPU limit.

Heap knobs

Prefer limit-aware sizing

Fixed

-Xmx768m

Clear, repeatable, but tied to one pod shape.

Relative

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60

Scales with the detected container limit.

Added in JDK 10 and backported to JDK 8u191; available in Java 17+.

Sizing rule

Assign MaxRAMPercentage from headroom


MaxRAMPercentage
  = (heap budget / container memory limit) * 100

heap budget
  = limit - observed native memory - safety margin

Measure native memory under load first; the percentage is the result, not the starting guess.

Example

Turn the budget into a flag


1Gi limit - 220Mi native - 190Mi margin = 614Mi heap

614Mi / 1024Mi = 60%

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60"

Use a lower percentage for thread-heavy, Netty/direct-buffer-heavy, or agent-heavy services.

Guardrails

How high should it be?

  • HotSpot's default max heap is 25% of detected memory.
  • That conservative default leaves room for native memory and other processes.
  • Start around 50-60% when native memory is unknown.
  • Move toward 65-75% only after NMT and cgroup usage stay stable under load.
  • Keep more headroom for small pods; fixed native costs consume a larger share.
  • Do not set -Xmx at the same time; it wins over percentage-based sizing.

Native headroom

The limit is not just heap


1Gi cgroup memory limit
  - 614Mi Java heap
  - 220Mi observed native memory
  = 190Mi safety margin

That native line includes threads, metaspace, direct buffers, code cache, GC, JIT, and libc allocations.

Native threads

Every OS thread brings a stack


500 OS threads * 1MiB stack = 500MiB reserved

# HotSpot Linux/x64 default is commonly 1024 KB per OS thread
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Xss512k"
# equivalent:
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:ThreadStackSize=512"

The JVM default is intentionally roomy. Lowering -Xss can reclaim native headroom when a process has many OS-backed threads.

Built-in tools

Native Memory Tracking gives you the map

  • Enable NMT with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary.
  • It adds native-allocation bookkeeping overhead; summary is lighter than detail.
  • Use jcmd against the running JVM.
  • Use it in load tests or targeted production windows, then start with the big buckets.

Java 17+ example

A useful NMT summary shape


$ jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
Total: reserved=2161MB, committed=902MB

- Java Heap (reserved=614MB, committed=614MB)
- Class     (reserved=1040MB, committed=82MB)
- Thread    (reserved=126MB, committed=18MB)
- Code      (reserved=248MB, committed=55MB)
- GC        (reserved=48MB,  committed=48MB)
- Compiler  (reserved=3MB,   committed=3MB)
- Internal  (reserved=18MB,  committed=18MB)
- Other     (reserved=64MB,  committed=64MB)

Heap appears here for context; the native budget is mostly everything outside Java Heap.

Read the buckets

Read one NMT bucket


- Thread (reserved=59260KB, committed=5588KB)
          (threads #29)
          (stack: reserved=59160KB, committed=5488KB)
          (malloc=68KB tag=Thread #175)
  • 29 JVM and application threads exist.
  • Stacks reserve about 58MiB of address space.
  • Only about 5.5MiB is committed right now.
  • Thread count and -Xss change this budget.

Read the buckets

What usually moves the number?

  • Class: many loaded classes, frameworks, proxies, or hot redeploy behavior.
  • Thread: large servlet pools, scheduler pools, Kafka consumers, or blocking I/O.
  • Code: lots of hot methods compiled by the JIT over time.
  • GC: bigger heaps, more regions, remembered sets, and collector worker data.
  • Other: direct buffers, Netty, compression, TLS, JNI, or native libraries.

Workflow

Get a picture in minutes


jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# run representative load
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff

The goal is not perfect accounting. The goal is to stop guessing.

Example

jcmd VM.info ties it together


$ jcmd 1 VM.info
container (cgroup) information:
    container_type: cgroupv2
    memory_limit_in_bytes: 1073741824
    memory_and_swap_limit_in_bytes: 1073741824
    cpu_quota: 100000
    cpu_period: 100000
    active_processor_count: 1

Capture this beside pod spec, heap settings, and load-test results.

Compare

jcmd plus NMT explains the gap


$ jcmd 1 GC.heap_info
garbage-first heap   total 629145600, used 402653184

$ jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
Total: reserved=1842MB, committed=832MB
- Java Heap (reserved=614MB, committed=614MB)
- Thread    (reserved=126MB, committed=18MB)
- Class     (reserved=1040MB, committed=82MB)
- Code      (reserved=248MB, committed=55MB)

GC.heap_info is collector-specific; NMT explains JVM categories to budget, and cgroup usage decides the kill.

Recent diagnostics

RSS alone is not the kill line

  • Containers account process memory plus cache.
  • JDK 23 and newer 17/21 updates add RSS and cache to jcmd VM.info and hs_err crash logs.
  • hs_err is the JVM's fatal-error report, often written as hs_err_pid*.log.
  • That makes post-OOM evidence line up better with Kubernetes limits.

Example

Newer diagnostics show cgroup usage


container (cgroup) memory:
    limit: 1073741824
    usage: 812388352
    rss: 641728512
    cache: 170659840

That cache segment explains why process RSS can be below the cgroup usage that triggers a kill.

Right-size loop

Measure, set, validate

  1. Confirm the JVM detects the pod's cgroup limits.
  2. Measure heap and native memory under realistic load.
  3. Set -Xmx or MaxRAMPercentage with explicit native headroom.
  4. Validate RSS, cache, and cgroup usage before production traffic does it for you.

Takeaways

A simple rule

  • Heap graphs do not explain the whole container.
  • Java 17+ gives you better container awareness, but you should verify it.
  • NMT, jcmd, JFR, and cgroup metrics are already in the JDK toolbox.
  • Right-sizing is cheaper when it starts with measurement.
